# Recursive Replacement

R<sup>2</sup>D defines microstate and macrostate relative to a count boundary.

That immediately creates a consequence:

> **When the boundary changes, the state domain changes.**

A state that is readable as a macrostate at one boundary does not remain the
same macrostate at the next boundary.

Its count meaning changes.

R<sup>2</sup>D calls this change in state domain **recursive replacement**.

Recursive replacement is not the disappearance of the subordinate physical
system.

It is the replacement of one boundary-defined state classification by another.

## Start With Boundary-Relative Statehood

At boundary \(B_n\), a macrostate \(i\) is readable.

Its formal microstates are compatible joint realizations of the immediately
subordinate peer boundaries:

$$
\mu_n
\in
\mathfrak{M}_n.
$$

The classification map

$$
\pi_n:
\mathfrak{M}_n
\rightarrow
\mathcal{M}_n
$$

assigns those compatible realizations to readable macrostates.

Thus,

$$
\pi_n(\mu_n)=i.
$$

Now change the boundary.

At \(B_{n+1}\), the formal microstate domain and classification map are
different.

The state \(i\) defined at \(B_n\) is no longer automatically a readable
macrostate at \(B_{n+1}\).

The count domain has changed.

Therefore the state identity has changed.

[Macrostate and Microstate →](macrostate-microstate.qmd)

## A State Is Not Carried Upward Unchanged

It is tempting to picture scale hierarchically:

$$
\text{small object}
\rightarrow
\text{larger object}
\rightarrow
\text{still larger object},
$$

while imagining that the smaller objects remain the same primitive state
variables at every level.

R<sup>2</sup>D proposes something different.

At each boundary, the readable states belong to that boundary.

Changing the boundary therefore gives:

$$
\boxed{
\text{state domain at } B_n
\rightarrow
\text{boundary change}
\rightarrow
\text{new state domain at } B_{n+1}
}
$$

The subordinate state can remain physically consequential.

But it does not remain the same readable state at the enclosing boundary.

> **Recursive replacement preserves consequence without preserving state
> identity.**

## A Coin Example

Consider one coin.

At the single-coin boundary \(B_{n-1}\), the readable macrostates are

$$
H
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
T.
$$

A transition such as

$$
H \rightarrow T
$$

is directly readable at that boundary.

Now consider an ensemble of ten such coins at \(B_n\).

The readable macrostate may instead be

$$
N_H=3.
$$

One compatible realization might be

$$
HHTTTHTTTT,
$$

while another might be

$$
THTTHTHTTT.
$$

At \(B_n\), both are classified as

$$
N_H=3.
$$

The individual assignment of heads and tails has not become the ensemble
macrostate.

It has been replaced by a new boundary-defined classification.

The ensemble does not ask:

> Which exact sequence of single-coin states exists?

It asks:

> Which ensemble state is readable here?

[The Coins Example →](coins.qmd)

## Replacement Is Many-to-One

Many subordinate realizations can correspond to one enclosing state.

For example,

$$
\mu_n^{(1)},
\mu_n^{(2)},
\mu_n^{(3)},
\dots
$$

may all satisfy

$$
\pi_n(\mu_n^{(r)})=i.
$$

Thus several distinguishable subordinate realizations become one readable
enclosing classification.

Schematically:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_n^{(1)} &\rightarrow i \\
\mu_n^{(2)} &\rightarrow i \\
\mu_n^{(3)} &\rightarrow i
\end{aligned}
$$

The enclosing state does not preserve enough information to reconstruct which
subordinate realization supplied it uniquely.

This is not an error.

It is what the enclosing state **is**.

Its multiplicity is

$$
W_{n,i}
=
\left|
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\right|.
$$

So multiplicity itself records the many-to-one structure of replacement.

[Multiplicity →](multiplicity.qmd)

## Replacement Is Not Destruction

Suppose a subordinate path is readable at \(B_n\).

After the boundary changes to \(B_{n+1}\), that path may no longer remain
individually readable.

This does not mean the subordinate realization never occurred.

Nor does it mean its physical consequences vanish.

The path remains defined relative to the boundary at which it was a readable
state relation.

What changes is its **count identity** at the enclosing boundary.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{subordinate state identity is replaced}
}
$$

while

$$
\boxed{
\text{the recursive relation can remain consequential}.
}
$$

This distinction becomes important throughout R<sup>2</sup>D.

## Replacement Is Not Coarse-Graining

Ordinary coarse-graining is often pictured as

$$
\text{same microscopic reality}
\rightarrow
\text{less detailed description}.
$$

The microscopic state remains the presumed primitive object.

Information about it is merely ignored, averaged, or unresolved.

R<sup>2</sup>D makes a stronger claim.

When the count boundary changes,

$$
\boxed{
\text{the classification itself changes}.
}
$$

The enclosing macrostate is not simply a lower-resolution version of the
subordinate state.

It belongs to a different state domain.

So the R<sup>2</sup>D sequence is

$$
\boxed{
\text{subordinate state}
\rightarrow
\text{boundary change}
\rightarrow
\text{replacement by enclosing statehood}.
}
$$

[Why R²D Is Not Coarse-Graining →](not-coarse-graining.qmd)

## Macrostate Here, Microstate There

The replacement becomes especially clear for transitions.

Suppose

$$
u \rightarrow v
$$

is readable as a macrostate transition at subordinate boundary
\(B_{n-1,\alpha}\).

Relative to the enclosing boundary \(B_n\), that same subordinate change
participates in a formal microstate transition.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{macrostate transition at } B_{n-1}
=
\text{microstate transition relative to } B_n.
}
$$

Nothing requires the physical occurrence itself to disappear.

Its count meaning changes because the boundary changes.

This is why "micro" and "macro" cannot designate absolute physical scales in
R<sup>2</sup>D.

They designate relations to a boundary.

## Replacement Changes What the Object Is

Consider a molecular motor.

At one boundary, a conformational state of a myosin molecule may be the
scientific object.

At another boundary, an ensemble distribution of myosin states may be the
scientific object.

At another, muscle force or shortening may define the readable state.

These are not increasingly blurry descriptions of one myosin molecule.

They are different boundary-defined scientific objects.

Schematically:

$$
\text{molecular state}
\rightarrow
\text{ensemble state}
\rightarrow
\text{muscle state}.
$$

Each arrow changes the count domain.

The subordinate relation remains necessary for realization.

But its state identity is replaced.

## Why This Matters in Biology

Biological systems make recursive replacement unusually visible because
several neighboring boundaries can often be experimentally accessed.

For example:

$$
\text{fast protein dynamics}
\rightarrow
\text{molecular switch state}
\rightarrow
\text{ensemble occupancy}
\rightarrow
\text{muscle-scale function}.
$$

At each stage, a new state domain becomes readable.

The faster subordinate trajectory does not remain the trajectory of the
larger-scale biological function.

Instead, many subordinate realizations can belong to one persistent
enclosing state.

This is why a protein structure, cellular state, or muscle state cannot be
identified with one privileged subordinate molecular trajectory.

## Replacement Is Recursive

There is no reason for the process to stop after one boundary change.

Suppose the hierarchy is

$$
B_{n-1}
\rightarrow
B_n
\rightarrow
B_{n+1}
\rightarrow
B_{n+2}.
$$

At every step:

1. a boundary defines its own readable states;
2. those states are realized through compatible subordinate relations;
3. changing to the enclosing boundary changes the state domain;
4. the subordinate state identity is replaced by a new enclosing
   classification.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{replacement}
\rightarrow
\text{replacement}
\rightarrow
\text{replacement}
\rightarrow \cdots
}
$$

This is why the framework is called **Recursively Realized
Distinguishability**.

The architecture repeats across boundaries.

## Replacement Does Not Mean Bottom-Up Construction

One must be careful with the direction implied by the diagram.

The sequence

$$
B_{n-1}
\rightarrow
B_n
\rightarrow
B_{n+1}
$$

does **not** mean that smaller states causally assemble themselves upward to
create larger states.

That would restore the bottom-up ontology R<sup>2</sup>D is trying to
distinguish from the count architecture.

The enclosing boundary defines which joint subordinate realizations are
compatible with its state.

Thus the causal relation is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{enclosing organization}
\Longrightarrow
\text{compatible subordinate realization}.
}
$$

The subordinate processes are necessary realizers.

They do not thereby become the primitive source of the enclosing
organization.

[The Causal Inversion →](causal-inversion.qmd)

## Two Directions Must Be Distinguished

This produces one of the most important distinctions in R<sup>2</sup>D.

There is a **causal direction**:

$$
\boxed{
\text{enclosing relation}
\Longrightarrow
\text{compatible local realization}.
}
$$

And there is a **change in count meaning** when the boundary changes:

$$
\boxed{
\text{completed local realization}
\mapsto
\text{enclosing classification}.
}
$$

These arrows point in opposite diagrammatic directions.

They do not describe opposite causal flows.

The first asks:

> **Which subordinate realizations are compatible with this enclosing
> relation?**

The second asks:

> **How is a completed subordinate realization counted when the boundary
> changes?**

The second operation is developed formally in R<sup>2</sup>D as
**recursive carry**.

[Recursive Carry →](recursive-carry.qmd)

## Replacement and Carry Are Related but Distinct

Recursive replacement describes the change of state domain itself.

A state readable at one boundary is not preserved as the same state when the
boundary changes.

Recursive carry describes how a completed realization at one boundary is
reclassified from the enclosing boundary.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{replacement}
=
\text{change in state domain}
}
$$

whereas

$$
\boxed{
\text{carry}
=
\text{change in count meaning of a completed realization}.
}
$$

Keeping these concepts separate prevents an important mistake.

Nothing has to be physically transported upward from one scale to another.

The relation is a change of classification.

## Replacement Preserves Multiplicity Consequence

Suppose several subordinate realizations are compatible with one enclosing
state.

Their individual identities may no longer be readable at the enclosing
boundary.

But the fact that many subordinate realizations belong to that state remains
mathematically consequential.

It appears as multiplicity.

Thus recursive replacement can remove readable subordinate identity while
preserving the count consequence of subordinate degeneracy.

This is one reason multiplicity is so central to R<sup>2</sup>D.

> **Identity can be replaced while count consequence remains.**

## A Recursive Counting Hierarchy

The resulting architecture can be summarized schematically:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{readable states at } B_{n-1}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{compatible realization at } B_n
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{readable states at } B_n
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{compatible realization at } B_{n+1}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{readable states at } B_{n+1}
\end{array}
}
$$

At no point must one fixed object retain the same state identity across the
entire hierarchy.

Instead, scientific objecthood is recursively replaced.

[Scientific Objecthood →](scientific-objecthood.qmd)

## Why Recursive Replacement Matters

Once recursive replacement is accepted, several familiar problems look
different.

### The observer problem

Increasing resolution changes the count boundary and therefore changes the
state classification.

### The many-body problem

The enclosing boundary can classify a joint subordinate realization without
preserving every peer trajectory as a readable state variable.

### Emergence

A larger-scale state need not be treated merely as shorthand for the same
microscopic object.

It is a state belonging to a different count domain.

### Reduction

Knowing every subordinate mechanism does not automatically specify the
enclosing state classification or the enclosing relation that organizes
those realizations.

### Cross-scale causality

A subordinate mechanism may be necessary for realization without being the
primitive source of the enclosing organization.

These are not separate additions to R<sup>2</sup>D.

They follow from the same boundary-relative definition of state.

## The Core Principle

Recursive replacement can be summarized in one statement:

> **Changing the count boundary changes what is being counted.**

Or more formally:

$$
\boxed{
B_n \rightarrow B_{n+1}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathcal{M}_n \not\equiv \mathcal{M}_{n+1}.
}
$$

The two boundaries define different state domains.

Therefore:

> **A subordinate state does not persist unchanged into an enclosing
> description. Its identity is replaced, while its recursive relation can
> remain consequential.**

That is recursive replacement.

---

## The Architecture So Far

R<sup>2</sup>D can now be summarized as:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{distinguishable states}
\rightarrow
\text{multiplicity}
\rightarrow
\text{occurrence and occupancy}
\rightarrow
\text{recursive replacement}.
}
$$

The next question is:

> **When a completed local realization is replaced at the enclosing
> boundary, how is it counted there?**

That is the problem of recursive carry.
